title: Returning to life
hookLine: after remembering, the tradition turns back toward life

cards: The week of mourning is over. In some families, on the last morning of shiva, the mourners stand up from their low chairs, open the front door, and walk around the block together.
The neighbors' houses look exactly the same. The mailman is on his round. A dog barks.
The mourners are not the same. The walk isn't forgetting. It's a first step back into a street that kept going while they sat.

teach.b: The Torah puts the choice plainly.

Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses calls heaven and earth to witness and tells the people: "I have set before thee life and death, the blessing and the curse; therefore choose life, that thou mayest live, thou and thy seed."
It's a command you can't keep once and be done, so the tradition builds it into its law and its habits.
The Talmud teaches that when a funeral procession and a wedding procession meet at a crossroads, the wedding goes first: the living, beginning something, have the right of way.

Saving a life sets aside nearly every other commandment, even Shabbat; the rabbis call this pikuach nefesh. And the toast raised at Jewish tables, at weddings and births and plain Friday nights, is short: l'chaim.
To life. Survivors lived this, some without words for it. They married.
They had children, and some named them after the people they had lost. They opened shops, planted gardens, danced at weddings. Not because they had moved on.
The names came with them, and the witness, and the questions. But the tradition sets the table again, pours the wine, says the blessing, and that too is a way of remembering.
Tomorrow the story turns to what came after the war.

how: Jewish mourning moves in stages back toward ordinary life; some families end shiva with a walk around the block, and Jews toast l'chaim, to life, at celebrations.

practice: Let these last few sessions settle, then choose one thing that gives life, watering a plant, cooking something warm, calling someone you love, walking outside, putting on music, and picture yourself doing it in detail.
If you pray, give thanks for life in the words of your own tradition; if not, simply notice the breath coming in and going out. That's life too.
